title: What time, what day
goal: Tell the time and the day, make appointments — and get the hang of a clock that counts forward from the hour, with a few extras English doesn't have.
bekal: say any time precisely, including quarters and thirds of an hour
name the days, and know when the Egyptian weekend falls

dialogs.title: حوار — مواعيد الأسبوع
dialogs.intro: Mona and Budi are planning when they can study together. Both of them open their phones.

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.text: نذاكر مع بعض إمتى؟ إيه رأيك في بكرة؟
lines.baca: nizaakir ma‘a ba‘ḍ imta? ’ēh ra’yak fi bukra?
lines.id: When shall we study together? How about tomorrow?
lines.literal: we-study with each-other when? what your-opinion in tomorrow?

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: التلات عندي درس لحد الساعة تلاتة.
lines.id: On Tuesday I have class until three.
lines.literal: the-third at-me lesson until the-hour three.

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.text: طيب، نتقابل الساعة أربعة إلا ربع؟
lines.baca: ṭayyib, nit’aabil is-saa‘a arba‘a illa rub‘?
lines.id: Okay, shall we meet at a quarter to four?
lines.literal: okay, we-meet the-hour four except quarter?

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.text: في مكتبة الجامعة. بتفتح لحد تمانية بالليل.
lines.baca: fi maktabit ig-gam‘a. bitiftah lihadd tamanya bil-lēl.
lines.id: At the university library. It's open until eight in the evening.
lines.literal: in library the-university. it-opens until eight at-the-night.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: تمام. بس ممكن أتأخر شوية، المترو زحمة.
lines.baca: tamaam. bas mumkin at’akhkhar shuwayya, il-mitro zahma.
lines.id: Perfect. But I might be a little late — the metro's packed.
lines.literal: complete. but possible I-am-late a-little, the-metro crowded.

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.id: Don't worry about it. I'll wait for you.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: And Thursday? Do you have time?

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.text: الخميس صعب. بروح البلد عند العيلة.
lines.id: Thursday's difficult. I go home to my family.
lines.literal: the-Thursday difficult. I-go the-hometown at the-family.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: Right, Friday and Saturday are the weekend here.

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.id: Yes. The week starts on Sunday.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: غريبة عليا لسه. عندنا السبت والحد شغل.
lines.id: Still strange for me. Back home Saturday and Sunday are days off.
lines.literal: strange on-me still. at-us the-Saturday and-the-Sunday work.

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.text: حتتعود. يلا، بكرة أربعة إلا ربع.
lines.baca: hatit‘awwid. yalla, bukra arba‘a illa rub‘.
lines.id: You'll get used to it. Okay, tomorrow at a quarter to four.
lines.literal: you-will-get-used. come-on, tomorrow four except quarter.

notes: **The word ونص means half PAST.** الساعة سبعة ونص means 7:30 — "seven and a half", just like British "half seven". Egyptian counts **forward** from the hour that has passed. If your own language says "half eight" for 7:30, as German or Dutch does, this is the place to be careful.
**The word إلا means "to", literally "except".** أربعة إلا ربع means 3:45 — a quarter to four. This is the only place Egyptian counts backwards, and only for the last quarter and third of the hour.

**Egyptian days are numbered, not named.** الاتنين is literally "the second", التلات "the third", الأربع "the fourth". Since the count starts on Sunday, the day is clear as soon as you know the number — so you've actually been able to name the days since unit five.

**The Egyptian weekend falls on Friday and Saturday**, and the working week starts on Sunday. This isn't just a calendar detail; it changes how every appointment is made. If you work remotely with Egyptians, their Sunday is your Monday.

**The word لحد means "until" or "as far as", for both time and place.** لحد الساعة تلاتة (until three o'clock), لحد المحطة (as far as the station). It combines لـ and حد, and it's used much more often than the Fusha حتى.
**The word زحمة means "crowded, jammed", and it's practically Cairo's official adjective.** الشارع زحمة، المترو زحمة، الدنيا زحمة. As a noun it means the traffic jam itself: فيه زحمة النهاردة.

grammars.title: Telling the time
body: The pattern always starts with the word الساعة, then the number in its stand-alone form, then the minutes added on.
after: Notice that Egyptian has a special word for **a third of an hour** — تلت, twenty minutes. English has nothing like it, and beginners often skip it even though it's heard as often as "quarter".
To tell morning from evening, add الصبح or بالليل after it: الساعة سبعة الصبح، الساعة سبعة بالليل. Midnight is نص الليل.
To ask: الساعة كام؟ (what time is it?) — and the same phrase is used to ask what time something happens; context tells them apart. To be clearer: حنتقابل الساعة كام؟

grammars.title: The days, and how they're numbered
body: Seven days, six of them simply numbers. Day names always take الـ.
after: Only two days have real names: الجمعة, the day people gather for Friday prayers, and السبت, which shares a root with the Jewish Sabbath — the same word that gave English *Sabbath*.
To say "on a day", just say the day with no preposition: بشتغل السبت (I work on Saturday). If it's every week, put كل in front, as in كل جمعة.

blocks.text: The phrase أنا في الطريق ("I'm on my way") deserves a note of its own. In Egypt it's said with a wide range of honesty, from "I'm at the door" to "I've just woken up". Don't be offended — and don't use it with the same latitude until you really know your circle.

blocks.title: Egyptian time, and how to read it
items: An 8:00 p.m. appointment in Cairo often means anywhere between eight and nine. That's not rudeness but a shared habit, and Egyptians understand each other perfectly.
What is **not** flexible: official appointments, office business, and the doctor. There, punctuality is fully expected.
If you really need precision, add بالظبط *biz-ẓabṭ* (exactly): الساعة تمانية بالظبط. It sounds firm and is understood as a serious request.

blocks.text: Egypt uses the Gregorian calendar for everyday life and the Hijri calendar for religious matters. Egyptian month names use the European forms, unlike the Levant, which uses ancient Semitic names.

Notice that the month names are almost the same as in English, because both come from Latin. The Hijri month you'll hear most is of course رمضان *ramaḍaan*, along with the two big holidays: عيد الفطر *‘iid il-fiṭr* and عيد الأضحى *‘iid il-aḍa*.

exercises.prompt: Write these times in Egyptian Arabic.

items: Let's meet at a quarter to four.
I might be a little late.
Do you have time tomorrow? (to a woman)

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

answers: الساعة خمسة. — الساعة ستة وربع. — الساعة تسعة ونص. — الساعة حداشر وتلت. — الساعة تلاتة إلا ربع.
الساعة كام دلوقتي؟ — نتقابل الساعة أربعة إلا ربع. — عندي درس لحد الساعة تلاتة. — ممكن أتأخر شوية. — عندك وقت بكرة؟
الساعة كام؟ — نتقابل الساعة أربعة إلا ربع. — عندي درس لحد الساعة تلاتة. — حاتأخر شوية والمترو زحمة. — الجمعة والسبت أجازة.
